timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In the book I talk a lot about leaning into the pain. Quite often we know what the right
thing to do is, but it seems difficult. We're afraid to do it. It seems unnatural. And
I experienced that as a prison of war. And that's one of the reasons I think that's
so important is I learned from that that you have to lean into the pain. You can't
always do what feels good and natural and easy. You can't always take the easy way
out. In fact most often the difficult decisions and the difficult choices are the
right ones. And we have to lean into the pain. And that occurred for me when I was
being interrogated and they wanted me to fill out a biography of my life
experience, my military experience and all that sort of stuff, background
information. And I refused to do it. Well of course when you refuse to do things
that the captors want you to do then they take offense to that and they had felt
like they had to punish me and they had to torture me to provide the
information which they did. And that was a very difficult time. The hardest part
for me was eventually I couldn't handle it anymore. And so I agreed to do
something. But I was still mentally in the fight and this is part of our guidance
from our leaders was you know we resist them, take torture to resist. But at
some point you have to you'll have to give in because you won't be able to
resist anymore. But you don't want to become a Bolognian in their hands where
you do whatever they want you to do. So you stop short of losing your ability to
stand the fight. But even then knowing that I had you know put up the good
fight and done my best I felt like a traitor. I mean I'm laying on the floor in
this filthy room you know in handcuffs and now in leg irons and I feel like
the weakest worst soldier military aviator that's everyone in the uniform
because I feel like I've let my country down my teammates down myself down my
own values. Of course later because of the support network and the
co-work communications we had and my cellmates they encouraged me and said hey
we've been there same thing happened to us you know bounce back be resilient and
that was important to know that they stood beside me they understood they had
been through the same thing and I was okay I wasn't going to be court
martial when I came home and that was a very difficult time but I learned a lot
from that that you just sometimes to do the right thing you have to press in to
your zone of discomfort and stick by your values and commitments.

youtube_description:
In this video interview, author and leadership coach, Lee Ellis, describes how important it is to lean into the pain of your fears and do the right thing. Leaders with a strong sense of character, courage, and competency can accomplish so much if they're equipped with the wisdom to do so, and our objective is restore honorable leadership in every sector of society. 

These observations were learned during Lee's POW experience in Vietnam described in his latest book, "Leading with Honor: Leadership Lessons from the Hanoi Hilton."

To learn more about the Leading with Honor or the publishing company, FreedomStar Media, go to www.LeadingWithHonor.com
